source_title: AMFI - Expense Ratio explainer
text:
Topic: AMFI - Expense Ratio explainer
Fact: Expense Ratio (part 1 of 2)
Under SEBI (Mutual Funds) Regulations, 1996, Mutual Funds are permitted to charge certain operating expenses for managing a mutual fund scheme – such as sales & marketing / advertising expenses, administrative expenses, transaction costs, investment management fees, registrar fees, custodian fees, audit fees – as a percentage of the fund’s daily net assets.
All such costs for running and managing a mutual fund scheme are collectively referred to as ‘Total Expense Ratio’ (TER)
The TER is calculated as a percentage of the Scheme’s average Net Asset Value (NAV). The daily NAV of a mutual fund is disclosed after deducting the expenses.
Currently, in India, the expense ratio is fungible, i.e., there is no limit on any particular type of allowed expense as long as the total expense ratio is within the prescribed limit. The regulatory limits of TER that can be incurred/charged to the fund by a Mutual Fund AMC have been specified under Regulation 52 of SEBI Mutual Fund Regulations.
Source: https://www.amfiindia.com/investor/knowledge-center-info?zoneName=expenseRatio
Scraped: 2026-11-01

source_title: AMFI - Expense Ratio explainer
text:
Topic: AMFI - Expense Ratio explainer
Fact: Expense Ratio (part 2 of 2)
Effective from April 1, 2020 the TER limit has been revised as follows.
In addition, mutual funds have been allowed to charge up to 30 bps more, if the new inflows from retail investors from beyond top 30 cities (B30) cities are at least (a) 30% of gross new inflows in the scheme or (b) 15% of the average assets under management (year to date) of the scheme, whichever is higher. This is essentially to encourage inflows into mutual funds from tier - 2 and tier - 3 cities.
TER has a direct bearing on a scheme’s NAV – the lower the expense ratio of a scheme, the higher the NAV . Thus, TER is an important parameter while selecting a mutual fund scheme.
As per the current SEBI Regulations, mutual funds are required to disclose the TER of all schemes on a daily basis on their websites as well as AMFI’s website.
Source: https://www.amfiindia.com/investor/knowledge-center-info?zoneName=expenseRatio

Investing is an essential part of personal finance, but it comes with its fair share of risks. This tool provides a clear and visual representation of the risk level associated with a particular mutual fund scheme, allowing investors to match their risk appetite with investment options.

Topic: SEBI Investor - Understanding the Riskometer
Fact: What is a Riskometer?
The Riskometer is a risk-measuring tool used in the mutual fund industry to depict the risk level of a mutual fund scheme. It is mandatory for asset management companies to display the Riskometer on their schemes as per guidelines by SEBI.
The Riskometer simplifies complex risk assessments, giving investors a snapshot of the potential risks involved in a fund, ranging from low to very high.
Source: https://investor.sebi.gov.in/riskometer.html

source_title: SEBI Investor - Understanding the Riskometer
text:
Topic: SEBI Investor - Understanding the Riskometer
Fact: How Does the Riskometer Work?
The Riskometer classifies mutual fund schemes into five risk categories:
Each level is color-coded to improve visual clarity for investors:
The classification is based on several factors, such as:
Low Risk: Investments are considered safe, with minimal volatility.
Low to Moderate Risk: Slightly higher risk than low-risk funds but still relatively stable.
Moderately High Risk: Investments with significant exposure to market volatility.
High Risk: Investment with higher risk than moderate.
Low Risk: Irish Green
Low to Moderate Risk: Chartreuse
Moderate Risk: Neon Yellow
Moderately High Risk: Caramel
High Risk: Dark Orange
Very High Risk: Red
The nature of the underlying assets (equity, debt, or hybrid).
Market volatility
Credit risk and interest rate sensitivity.
Source: https://investor.sebi.gov.in/riskometer.html

source_title: SEBI Investor - Understanding the Riskometer
text:
Topic: SEBI Investor - Understanding the Riskometer
Fact: Benefits of the Riskometer (part 1 of 2)
Risk Assessment: The Riskometer helps investors gauge the risk level of a mutual fund scheme before investing.
Decision Making: Investors can align their risk appetite with the right fund category.
Transparency: It ensures that mutual funds are transparent about their risk levels, fostering trust.
Simplification: The visual representation is easy to understand, making it accessible to novice investors.
Informed Decisions: It helps investors choose funds that match their financial goals and risk tolerance.
Standardized Tool: Being a regulatory mandate, it ensures consistency across all fund houses.
Prevention of Mismatched Investments: Avoids scenarios where low-risk investors end up in high-risk schemes inadvertently.
The risk levels are reviewed periodically and updated based on changing market conditions
Fund houses must include the Riskometer in their fact sheets and promotional materials.
It applies to all mutual fund categories, including equity, debt, and hybrid funds.
Source: https://investor.sebi.gov.in/riskometer.html

text:
Topic: SEBI Investor - A Guide to ELSS
Fact: A Guide to ELSS (Equity-Linked Savings Scheme)
Equity-Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS) is a type of mutual fund designed specifically for individuals seeking tax savings under Section 80C of the Income Tax Act, 1961.
ELSS has gained popularity due to its dual advantage of tax efficiency and wealth creation over the long term. It is an ideal choice for those who are comfortable with market-linked investments and aim to build wealth while saving on taxes.
Source: https://investor.sebi.gov.in/elss.html

source_title: SEBI Investor - A Guide to ELSS
text:
Topic: SEBI Investor - A Guide to ELSS
Fact: Meaning of ELSS
An ELSS is a diversified equity mutual fund where at least 80% of the corpus is invested in equity and equity-related instruments. It has a lock-in period of three years, which is the shortest among all tax-saving investment options under Section 80C.
Source: https://investor.sebi.gov.in/elss.html

Topic: SEBI Investor - A Guide to ELSS
Fact: How ELSS Works
Investment: Investors can invest a lump sum or opt for a Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) to contribute small amounts regularly.
Lock-in Period: Once invested, the amount is locked in for three years. During this period, you cannot withdraw the funds.
Tax Deduction: Under Section 80C, an investment of up to ₹1.5 lakh in ELSS qualifies for a tax deduction in a financial year.
Source: https://investor.sebi.gov.in/elss.html
Scraped: 2026-11-01

Topic: SEBI Investor - A Guide to ELSS
Fact: Benefits of ELSS
Tax Savings : ELSS is a preferred option for those looking to reduce their taxable income.
Discipline : The lock-in period ensures disciplined investing and prevents impulsive withdrawals.
Flexibility : Investors can opt for SIP or lump sum investments, depending on their financial goals and cash flow.
Professional Management : The fund is managed by experienced professionals, ensuring informed investment decisions

Topic: SEBI Investor - A Guide to ELSS
Fact: Key Features of ELSS
Equity Exposure: Invests predominantly in equity and equity-related instruments.
Minimum Investment: Investors can start with as low as Rs. 500.
Risk Factor: Being equity-based, it comes with market risks, which can be mitigated through long-term investment.
Growth and Dividend Options: Investors can choose between growth (capital appreciation) and dividend (periodic pay-outs) options.
Tax Efficiency: Provides dual tax benefits under Section 80C and through LTCG tax exemptions.
Source: https://investor.sebi.gov.in/elss.html
